reference_title: Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements

sections.title: Construction with Portland Cement
sections.summary: Soil-cement construction thoroughly mixes pulverized soil and cement in correct proportions with moisture for maximum compaction, via a simple, specific sequence: shape/scarify/pre-wet/precompact, then spread cement, add water, mix, compact, finish, cure.
sections.body: In soil-cement construction, the objective is to thoroughly mix a pulverized soil material and cement in correct proportions with moisture to permit maximum compaction. Construction methods are simple and follow a specific procedure: initial preparation (shape to crown and grade; scarify/pulverize/pre-wet if necessary; reshape; precompact), then processing (spread portland cement and mix; apply water as needed to reach optimum moisture; mix additive and soil thoroughly; compact; finish; cure). The remainder of this section covers the mixing equipment, cement handling/spreading equipment, the detailed construction sequence (preparation through curing, construction joints, and multiple-layer construction), and special construction problems (rainfall, wet soils, cold weather).
key_points: Initial preparation sequence: shape to crown/grade -> scarify/pulverize/pre-wet -> reshape -> precompact
Processing sequence: spread cement and mix -> apply water to optimum moisture -> mix thoroughly -> compact -> finish -> cure
Sub-topics covered: mixing equipment (4-1.2), cement handling/spreading equipment (4-1.3), full construction sequence (4-1.4), special problems (4-1.5)
sections.applicability: Governing section for all portland-cement stabilized-soil construction in the field.

sections.title: General Construction Steps
sections.summary: Same as 4-1's overview: initial preparation (shape/scarify/pre-wet/reshape/precompact) then processing (spread cement, add water, mix, compact, finish, cure) -- a fixed, simple sequence regardless of equipment.
sections.body: In soil-cement construction, the objective is to thoroughly mix a pulverized soil material and cement in correct proportions with moisture to permit maximum compaction. Construction methods are simple and follow a specific procedure. Initial preparation: (1) shape the area to crown and grade; (2) if necessary, scarify, pulverize, and pre-wet the soil; (3) reshape to crown and grade; (4) precompact. Processing: (1) spread portland cement and mix; (2) apply water, if necessary, to achieve the optimum moisture content; (3) mix the additive and soil thoroughly; (4) compact; (5) finish; (6) cure.
key_points: Preparation steps: shape to crown/grade, scarify/pulverize/pre-wet, reshape, precompact
Processing steps: spread cement and mix, apply water to optimum moisture, mix thoroughly, compact, finish, cure
The sequence is fixed regardless of which mixing equipment (traveling mixer or central plant) is used
sections.applicability: The baseline step sequence that all soil-cement construction methods (Sec 4-1.2-4-1.4) follow.

sections.title: Mixing Equipment
sections.summary: Soil, cement, and water are mixed in place (traveling mixers: transverse single-shaft mixer or windrow-type pugmill) or at a central mixing plant (continuous-flow or batch-type pugmill). Highly plastic clays are hardest to pulverize/mix; run trial batches to confirm feasibility.
sections.body: Soil, cement, and water can be mixed in place using traveling mixing machines (transverse single-shaft mixer or windrow-type pugmill) or mixed in a central mixing plant (continuous flow-type pugmill or batch-type pugmill). Regardless of equipment type, the general principles and objectives are the same. Certain soil materials cannot be pulverized and mixed in central mixing plants because of high silt/clay content and plasticity; if uncertain, run a trial batch. Almost all soil materials, from granular to fine-grained, can be adequately pulverized and mixed with transverse-shaft mixers given proper moisture control -- the exception is material containing predominantly highly plastic clays, which may require more mixing effort. Revolving-blade central mixing plants and traveling pugmills suit non-plastic to slightly plastic granular soils; a rotary-drum mixer suits coarse, non-plastic granular materials (though a small amount of slightly plastic fines may cause inadequate mixing). For plastic soils, thorough pulverization prior to mixing is important to reduce clod size, since smaller particle size increases specific surface area and improves additive coating/penetration.
key_points: Traveling mixing machines: transverse single-shaft mixer, windrow-type pugmill
Central mixing plants: continuous flow-type pugmill, batch-type pugmill
Transverse-shaft mixers can handle almost all soil types except predominantly highly plastic clays
Rotary-drum mixers suit coarse, non-plastic granular materials; may struggle with even slightly plastic fines
Thorough pulverization of plastic soils increases specific surface area, improving additive coating/penetration
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting mixing equipment (traveling mixer vs. central plant, and specific machine type) for a soil-cement project.

sections.title: Equipment for Handling and Spreading Cement
sections.summary: Bulk cement is spread by mechanical bulk spreaders (blanket type or windrow-deposit type) for mixed-in-place work; bagged cement suits small jobs. Central mixing plants meter cement via belt/screw/vane (continuous-flow) or batch weighing (batch/rotary-drum mixers).
sections.body: There are a number of methods for handling cement. For mixed-in-place construction using traveling mixing machines, bulk cement is spread on the area to be processed in required amounts by mechanical bulk cement spreaders; bag cement is permissible on jobs too limited in size to require mass quantities. Cement spreaders for mix-in-place construction are of two general types: those that spread cement over the soil material in a blanket, and those that deposit cement on top of a partially flattened or slightly trenched windrow of soil material. For centrally mixed soil-cement projects, cement meters on continuous-flow central mixing plants are of three types: belt with strikeoff, screw, or vane. The cement for batch-type pugmill mixers and rotary drum-mixers is batch weighed.
key_points: Mixed-in-place bulk spreaders: blanket-type or windrow-deposit type
Bagged cement: suited to small jobs not requiring mass quantities
Continuous-flow central plant cement meters: belt-with-strikeoff, screw, or vane type
Batch-type pugmill and rotary-drum mixers: cement is batch weighed rather than metered continuously
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting cement handling/spreading equipment appropriate to project scale and mixing method.

sections.title: Construction (Preparation Through Curing, Joints, Multi-Layer)
sections.summary: Construction with soil-cement is two steps -- preparation and processing -- requiring an adequately compacted, thorough mix of pulverized soil, correct cement, and moisture, then proper curing. Covers preparation, mixing/water application by machine type, compaction, finishing, curing, joints, and multi-layer builds.
sections.body: Construction with soil cement involves two steps: preparation and processing. PREPARATION: check crown/grade before construction starts (grade at the start largely determines final grade, since processing displaces little material); compact/shape the subgrade before placing any borrow material and correct soft areas; check equipment condition; use guide stakes/string lines; arrange adequate cement/water delivery. Pre-wetting the soil before cement application often saves processing time. Friable granular materials need little scarification; silty/clayey soils may need extra pulverization effort (dry brittle soils break down with added water; sticky soils pulverize more easily when slightly dried). Most specs require 100 percent of the mix passing a 1-in (25 mm) sieve and >= 80 percent passing the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve at compaction time (exclusive of gravel/stone, which must be <= 2 in / 50 mm maximum size). PROCESSING (equipment-specific mixing/water application): with a WINDROW-TYPE traveling mixer, prepared soil is bladed into uniform windrows, cement spread on top, then the mixer dry-mixes with the first paddles before water is added via spray nozzles and the remaining paddles complete mixing; a strike-off spreads the mixed soil-cement (a motor grader plus tamping roller is an alternative). With a SINGLE-SHAFT traveling mixer, only crown/grade shaping is needed (plus pre-wetting/scarifying if the roadbed is hard); mixing moisture 2-3 percentage points below optimum eases mixing (very sandy material tolerates 1-2 points above optimum); cement is spread by mechanical spreader or bags, and the mixer picks up soil and cement, mixing in place with water applied by spray bar or ahead of the mixer. With a CENTRAL MIXING PLANT (twin-shaft continuous-flow pugmill common on highway projects), friable granular borrow is preferred for low cement requirements/ease of handling; do not allow more than 60 minutes (usually limited to 30 minutes) between the start of moist-mixing and start of compaction; spread to full roadway width by one or more spreaders, compact immediately behind the spreader, and dampen the subgrade immediately before placing the mix. COMPACTION: compact at optimum moisture to maximum density and finish immediately; tamping rollers are typical for initial compaction (self-propelled/vibratory/pneumatic also used), with unit pressures from 75-125 lb/in2 (friable silty/clayey sands) up to 150-300 lb/in2 (medium-heavy clays/gravelly soils); compacted lift thickness up to 8-9 in (200-230 mm) in one lift; start compaction as soon as possible after mixing since cement hydration begins on contact with moisture. Trench-type and featheredge-type cross-sections are both used; do not build edge slopes steeper than 2:1. FINISHING: meet compaction/moisture/surface requirements; if needed, scarify (scratch) smooth surfaces (tire imprints, blade marks) to remove compaction planes, except on gravelly mixtures; keep the surface damp; a final light water application plus pneumatic-tired rolling seals the surface. CURING: a moisture-retaining cover (most commonly bituminous emulsion SS-1, applied at 0.15-0.30 US gal/sq yd / 0.68-1.36 L/sq m; also polymer emulsion, waterproof paper/plastic, wet straw/sand, fog spray, or wet burlap/mats) is placed soon after completion to retain moisture for cement hydration. CONSTRUCTION JOINTS: form a transverse vertical construction joint at the end of each day's work by cutting back into the completed soil-cement to proper crown/grade (via the mixer or a dry-cut saw); clean and re-trim the joint before continuing, leave it slightly high until final rolling/trimming. MULTIPLE-LAYER CONSTRUCTION: when specified thickness exceeds what can be compacted in one layer (usually 8-9 in / 200-230 mm), build multiple layers each less than 4 in (100 mm) thick; the lower layer need not be finished to exact grade; take care to eliminate raw-soil seams between layers.
key_points: Preparation: crown/grade check, subgrade compaction/shaping, equipment check, pre-wetting; pulverization spec typically 100% passing 1in, >=80% passing No.4
Windrow-type mixer: dry-mix first, then spray water, then finish mixing, strike-off spreads the mix
Single-shaft mixer: crown/grade shaping only; mixing moisture ~2-3 points below optimum for most soils
Central plant: haul time between moist-mixing start and compaction limited to 60 min (usually 30 min); spread and compact immediately
Compaction: tamping rollers typical, unit pressure 75-300 lb/in2 by soil type; lift thickness up to 8-9 in; compact ASAP after mixing (hydration starts on contact with moisture)
Curing: moisture-retaining cover soon after completion, most commonly bituminous emulsion SS-1 at 0.15-0.30 gal/sq yd
Construction joints: cut back to a clean vertical transverse joint at the end of each day's work
Multiple-layer construction: layers < 4 in (100 mm) each when total thickness exceeds single-lift capacity
sections.applicability: The complete field construction sequence for soil-cement, from initial preparation through curing and special conditions like joints and multi-layer builds.

sections.title: Special Construction Problems
sections.summary: Rainfall: crown/trench to shed water; if rain begins during cement spreading, stop and quickly mix in the cement already placed; compacted/finished soil-cement is unharmed by rain. Wet soils: dry by aeration; clayey soils need below-optimum moisture for mixing. Cold weather: do not place below 40F; protect from freezing 7 days.
sections.body: RAINFALL: crown loose/pulverized soil to shed water and trench low places to drain; construction typically requires water equivalent to 1-1.5 in (25-37.5 mm) of rain, so brief rain rarely causes serious problems. If rain falls during cement-spreading, stop spreading and quickly mix the already-spread cement into the soil mass; a heavy rainfall after most water has been added can be serious, so avoid letting placement/mixing outpace compaction (usually the slowest step) -- if rain becomes imminent, use every available piece of equipment for rapid compaction. After the mixture is compacted and finished, rain will not harm it. WET SOILS: cement can mix with sandy materials up to 2 percent above optimum moisture with adequate results, but clayey soils need moisture below optimum for efficient mixing; dry excessively wet material by aeration (raised-hood single-shaft mixers, or cutting/working with a motor-grader blade and disc). Maintaining crown/grade for rapid runoff is the best insurance against excess wet material. COLD WEATHER: cement hydration practically ceases near/below freezing; do not place soil-cement at 40 degF (4.4 degC) or below, and protect placed material from freezing for seven days (or until hardened) with a covering such as hay or straw.
key_points: Rainfall: crown/trench to shed water; stop cement spreading and mix in already-placed cement if rain begins; finished/compacted soil-cement is unaffected by subsequent rain
Wet soils: sandy soils tolerate mixing up to 2% above optimum moisture; clayey soils need below-optimum moisture; dry via aeration if needed
Cold weather: do not place soil-cement at or below 40F (4.4C); protect from freezing for 7 days after placement
sections.applicability: Applies to soil-cement construction under adverse weather (rain, excess soil moisture, or near-freezing temperatures).

sections.title: Construction with Lime
sections.summary: Three recognized lime-stabilization construction methods: in-place mixing, plant mixing, and pressure injection, each detailed in the child sections along with the standard construction step sequence.
sections.body: There are three recognized lime-stabilization methods: in-place mixing, plant mixing, and pressure injection.
key_points: In-place mixing (Sec 4-2.1): on-site or off-site-then-transported mixing of lime with soil/borrow
Plant mixing: soil hauled to a central plant where lime/soil/water are uniformly mixed
Pressure injection: lime slurry injected to depth for swelling/unstable soil control
sections.applicability: Governing section for all lime-stabilized soil construction in the field.

sections.title: Lime Stabilization Methods
sections.summary: In-place mixing (single/double lime increment, with or without a mellowing period, to depths up to 24in via deep-stabilization plows/mixers), plant mixing (predetermined lime content, hauled to site), and pressure injection (slurry to 7-10 ft depth on 5-ft spacing for swelling/unstable soils).
sections.body: IN-PLACE MIXING subdivides into: mixing lime with existing materials in place; off-site mixing of lime with borrow, then transport and final manipulation/compaction on site; and hauling borrow to the site for in-place processing. Variants: (1) one lime increment added to easily-pulverized clays/granular base, mixed and compacted in one operation, no mellowing needed; (2) one increment added with 1-7 days of mellowing to help break down heavy clay soils; (3) one increment for soil modification/pulverization ahead of cement or asphalt treatment; (4) one increment to produce a working table (proof-rolled instead of density-tested); (5) two increments (with mellowing between) for soils extremely difficult to pulverize; (6) deep stabilization to 18-24 in (460-600 mm) using plows/rippers/heavy disc harrows to break down clay chunks, with mechanical mixers pulverizing in progressive-depth passes (e.g. 6/9/12/15/18 in) and vibratory/conventional heavy rollers compacting from the top -- normal 8-9 in (200-230 mm) lifts should still be used near the pavement surface; deep mixing is not routine for airfield projects. PLANT MIXING: soil is hauled to a central plant where lime, soil, and water are uniformly mixed, then transported to the site for further manipulation; lime amount is usually predetermined by testing, though field adjustments may be needed for changing soil conditions. PRESSURE INJECTION: lime slurry injected to depths of 7-10 ft (2.1-3 m), typically on 5-ft (1.5 m) spacing with horizontal slurry seams at 8-12 in (200-300 mm) intervals, for swelling/unstable soil control under highways/buildings; the top 6-12 in (150-300 mm) layer is still stabilized by conventional methods.
key_points: In-place variants range from single-increment (no mellowing) to two-increment (with mellowing) to deep stabilization (18-24 in via progressive-depth mechanical mixing)
Deep stabilization compacts from the top with vibratory/heavy rollers; NOT routine for airfield projects
Plant mixing: lime content usually predetermined by testing; hauled/transported for final manipulation
Pressure injection: slurry to 7-10 ft depth, 5-ft spacing, 8-12 in vertical seam spacing, for swelling/unstable soil control
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting among in-place mixing, plant mixing, or pressure injection for a specific lime-stabilization project's depth and soil conditions.

sections.title: Construction Steps (Lime)
sections.summary: Soil preparation (grade adjustment for lime 'fluff'), lime application (dry hydrated lime, dry quicklime, or slurry -- each with trade-offs), pulverization/mixing (one- or two-stage), compaction (95%/90% ASTM D698 subbase/base, near-optimum moisture), and curing (moist or membrane).
sections.body: SOIL PREPARATION: bring subgrade to final grade/alignment, allowing for potential 'fluff' (volume increase) when lime-treated soil is mixed with water, especially at moisture below optimum; for fluff-prone soils, lower the subgrade elevation slightly or trim excess material (removing the top 0.25 in / 6 mm, which is often poorly reacted). Rip/scarify before or after dry lime is added; scarify before adding lime if slurry form is used. LIME APPLICATION: DRY HYDRATED LIME can be bagged (simplest, costliest, best for small jobs) or bulk (self-unloading auger or pneumatic transport trucks, spread by mechanical spreaders, downspouts, or boots -- pneumatic trucks are now most common, with fingertip cab controls for spreading width). DRY QUICKLIME requires extra safety care (anhydrous, exothermic on water contact, causes burns) -- provide a documented safety program (PPE, eyewash) and enforce it. SLURRY (hydrated lime or quicklime mixed with water) is popular where dust is a problem; a typical mix is 1 ton (907 kg) lime to 500 gal (1893 L) water yielding ~600 gal (2271 L) slurry at 31% lime solids (40% solids is the practical pumping maximum); spread by gravity or pressure spray bars (pressure preferred). DOUBLE APPLICATION (2-3% lime, mellow up to a week, then remainder) suits extremely plastic clay (PI 50+). Trade-offs: dry hydrated lime applies 2-3x faster than slurry and dries soil effectively, but dusts; dry quicklime is more economical (25% more free lime) with faster drying/reaction, but field-hydration gives coarser/poorer distribution, needs more water, and poses more burn risk; slurry is dust-free with better distribution and combined spreading/watering, but is slower and needs more equipment/cost. PULVERIZATION AND MIXING: heavy clays may need two-stage mixing (preliminary mix, 24-48 hr moist curing/mellowing with clods kept under 2 in / 50 mm, then final mixing/remixing via high-speed rotary mixers or one-pass travel plant mixers -- motor graders are generally unsatisfactory for heavy clays); other soils may use one-stage mixing (blade and/or rotary, rotary preferred for uniformity/fine pulverization). Typical spec: 100% passing 1 in (25 mm), 60% passing No. 4 (4.75 mm), exclusive of nonslaking fractions. COMPACTION: at least 95% of ASTM D698 for subbase and 90% for base (roads/non-traffic; often 95% ASTM D1557 for airfields); sheepsfoot roller until it 'walks out,' then multiple-wheel pneumatic roller is the most common practice; granular soil-lime compacts within 2 days of mixing without harm, fine-grained soil-lime within 4 days; longer delays (2+ weeks) may need ~0.5% additional lime to compensate for carbonation/erosion losses. CURING: moist curing (light sprinkling + light rolling) or asphaltic membrane curing (asphalt seal at 0.10-0.25 gal/sq yd / 0.45-1.13 L/sq m, possibly multiple applications); some specs require 3-7 days undisturbed curing, though immediate paving-layer placement is permitted if the compacted layer isn't rutted (the overlying course itself maintains curing moisture).
key_points: Soil prep: account for lime-induced 'fluff' (volume increase); trim the poorly-reacted top ~0.25 in after mixing

Dry hydrated lime: fast application but dusty; dry quicklime: economical/fast but coarser distribution and burn hazard requiring a documented safety program; slurry: dust-free, better distribution, but slower/costlier
Two-stage mixing (heavy clays): preliminary mix -> 24-48 hr mellow (clods < 2in) -> final mix via rotary mixer
Compaction: >= 95% ASTM D698 subbase, >= 90% base (often 95% D1557 for airfields); begin ASAP, max ~1 week delay per National Lime Association
Curing: moist curing (sprinkling+rolling) or asphaltic membrane curing (0.10-0.25 gal/sq yd); phenolphthalein indicator (pink at pH 12.4) is used for lime-presence/uniformity field checks
sections.applicability: The complete field construction sequence for lime-stabilized soil, from grade preparation through curing.

sections.title: Construction with Lime-Fly Ash (LF) and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash (LCF)
sections.summary: LF/LCF construction procedures resemble lime stabilization. Both field in-place and central plant mixing may be used, though central plant is recommended for adequate proportioning/mixing; LCF's cement content requires compaction as soon as possible.
sections.body: Construction procedures for LF and LCF are similar to those used for lime stabilization. Although both field in-place and central plant mixing may be used with LF and LCF, the latter procedure is recommended to obtain adequate proportioning and mixing. With LCF, note that the presence of cement requires the stabilized mixture be compacted as soon as possible.
key_points: Construction procedures largely mirror lime stabilization (Sec 4-2)
Central plant mixing is recommended over field in-place mixing for adequate proportioning of the multi-component LF/LCF mix
LCF's cement component requires compaction as soon as possible after mixing (hydration timing, as with plain soil-cement)
sections.applicability: Applies to LF and LCF stabilized-soil construction; defers to Sec 4-2 (lime) procedures except where noted.

sections.title: Construction with Bitumen or Polymer Emulsion
sections.summary: Bituminous stabilization can be hot-mix (similar to asphalt concrete, not detailed here) or cold-mix, mixed in place or in a central plant. Foamed bitumen (water injected into hot bitumen) is an efficient in-place technique; cutback asphalts are generally avoided for environmental/health reasons.
sections.body: Bituminous stabilization can involve either hot-mix or cold-mix materials. Bitumen and aggregate or soil can be blended in place or in a central plant. Construction procedures presented in this UFC are for cold-mix materials that are mixed in place (asphalt or polymer emulsions) or in a central plant; hot-mix hot-laid construction procedures are similar to those used for asphalt concrete and follow applicable standard construction procedures. Foamed bitumen stabilization is an in-place technique that injects water into hot bitumen to create a foaming effect that efficiently coats soil particles. The use of cutback asphalts (asphalt mixed with a solvent such as diesel or naphtha) is generally not acceptable due to environmental and health safety concerns. Procedures described in this chapter are applicable to a variety of liquid stabilizers.
key_points: Hot-mix hot-laid: follows standard asphalt concrete construction procedures (not detailed here)
Cold-mix: mixed in place or in a central plant; this UFC's procedures target cold-mix
Foamed bitumen: water injected into hot bitumen creates foam that efficiently coats soil particles, in-place technique
Cutback asphalts are generally NOT acceptable due to environmental/health safety concerns
sections.applicability: Governing section for all bituminous and polymer-emulsion stabilized-soil construction in the field.

sections.title: Equipment for Mixed-in-Place Materials
sections.summary: Special mixed-in-place bituminous equipment: travel plants (self-propelled pugmills), rotary-type mixers (most common; reclaimer-stabilizer machines with liquid injection systems are most versatile), motor graders (blade mixing, slow/less efficient), and liquid distributors (key for non-LIS rotary mixers or blade mixing).
sections.body: Some equipment used for mixed-in-place bituminous stabilization (water distributors, compaction equipment, graders, windrow sizers) is standard and not detailed here; only equipment with special features for liquid stabilization is discussed. TRAVEL PLANTS are self-propelled pugmill plants that proportion and mix aggregate/asphalt as they move along the road (windrow-picking type or hopper-fed type); a less common method. ROTARY-TYPE MIXERS are the most common form of stabilization, a mobile mixing chamber (6-8 ft / 1.8-2.4 m wide, open bottom) with a rotating drum of cutting blades/milling teeth; a reclaimer-stabilizer machine is the most versatile (can mill asphalt and mix most soils), a dedicated soil mixer is less powerful (tines only). Most single-shaft mixers have a liquid injection system (LIS) synchronizing liquid flow rate with travel speed for accurate dosing; without an LIS, use a liquid distributor spraying ahead of the mixer. Foamed asphalt stabilization uses a reclaimer-stabilizer machine specially outfitted for foamed-asphalt injection. MOTOR GRADERS perform blade mixing (on-site mixing on the roadbed) -- a common but slower, less efficient form of in-place mixing; equip with a blade >= 10 ft (3 m) and wheelbase >= 15 ft (4.6 m), smooth (not treaded) tires for finishing; not generally recommended for bitumen/polymer mixing due to pocket formation of unmixed additive. The LIQUID DISTRIBUTOR (truck or trailer-mounted insulated tank, heating system, pump, spray bar) is key for rotary mixers lacking a built-in LIS, or for blade mixing; keep an adequate liquid supply near the jobsite (bulk supply truck in rural areas).
key_points: Travel plants: self-propelled pugmill plants mixing aggregate/asphalt while moving along the road; less common
Rotary-type mixers: most common; reclaimer-stabilizer machines (most versatile) vs. dedicated soil mixers (tines only, less powerful)
Liquid injection system (LIS): synchronizes liquid flow with travel speed for accurate dosing; foamed asphalt uses a specially outfitted reclaimer-stabilizer
Motor graders (blade mixing): slower, less efficient, generally not recommended for bitumen/polymer due to additive pockets
Liquid distributor: essential for non-LIS rotary mixers or blade mixing; truck/trailer-mounted with spray bar
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting mixed-in-place equipment for bituminous or polymer-emulsion stabilization.

sections.title: Mixed-in-Place Construction
sections.summary: Windrow measurement/control, correct liquid application rate/moisture targeting (below optimum for polymer emulsion), viscosity/temperature control (no mixing below 50F aggregate), mixing method (travel plant, rotary, or blade -- each with its own procedure), aeration, then spreading/compacting.
sections.body: WINDROWS: several cold-mix methods require aggregate placed in windrows before mixing/spreading; clear vegetation for windrow-plus-traffic width; accurate windrow volume control is critical since new-pavement thickness is directly proportional to windrowed aggregate volume; blade loose road-surface material to the shoulder if there's not enough for the mix, or incorporate it if uniform and sufficient. DETERMINING APPLICATION RATE: before mixing, set the correct liquid application rate and mixer/distributor forward speed for the windrowed aggregate quantity; moisten aggregate before applying emulsion; for polymer emulsions, keep starting soil moisture WELL BELOW optimum (the emulsion's own water will otherwise push total moisture above optimum, lowering compacted density) -- asphalt emulsion tolerates this better since the asphalt coating itself lubricates for compaction. CONTROL OF LIQUID STABILIZERS: close control of quantity, dilution, and viscosity is required; cutback/emulsified asphalts may need heating to reach spray viscosity; do not mix at aggregate temperatures below 50 degF (10 degC). MIXING: TRAVEL-PLANT mixing offers the closest control -- match liquid rate to course width/thickness/mixer forward speed/aggregate density (forward speed is usually the variable); split into multiple windrows if one pass can't incorporate all the liquid; additional motor-grader mixing/aeration may follow. ROTARY MIXING (with LIS) requires accurate liquid-rate matching to width/thickness/forward speed/target stabilizer and moisture content; without a spraybar, use a liquid distributor ahead of the mixer with incremental passes; keep water-based-stabilizer soil moisture well below optimum. Foamed asphalt stabilization (via reclaimer-stabilizer) is best for sandy/gravelly soils and full-depth reclamation of old asphalt. BLADE MIXING uses a slow-setting liquid: shape a measured windrow, flatten to spraybar width, apply liquid via successive distributor passes with blade working between passes, reforming the windrow each time; watch for 'additive balls' (concentrated saturated fine-aggregate clusters) -- correctable for bitumen/cutback by tight-windrowing and curing a few days, but harder to correct for polymer emulsion (obtain a rotary mixer instead if balling persists). AERATION: for emulsified asphalts/polymers, begin compaction as the emulsion starts to 'break' (brown-to-black color change) or immediately after mixing (polymer); for cutback asphalt, aerate until volatile content drops to ~50% of the original and moisture <= 2% by weight, evidenced by the mix becoming tacky and 'crawling' -- fine-grained/well-graded mixes need longer aeration than open-graded/coarse mixes. SPREADING AND COMPACTING: spread to uniform thickness (no thin spots); mixtures not needing aeration can be spread and compacted immediately; mixtures needing aeration are windrowed then blade-spread in layers no thinner than ~1.5x the maximum particle diameter, compacting each layer immediately with a pneumatic-tired roller; finish-roll with a steel-wheeled roller until roller marks are eliminated; a diluted slow-setting emulsion seal coat (~0.10 gal/sq yd / 0.45 L/sq m) or sanding prevents tire pickup if opened to traffic early.
key_points: Windrow volume must be accurately controlled -- new pavement thickness is directly proportional to it
Polymer emulsions require starting soil moisture WELL BELOW optimum (unlike asphalt emulsion, which tolerates it better)
Do not mix at aggregate temperatures below 50F (10C)
Three mixing methods: travel-plant (closest control), rotary (LIS or liquid-distributor-fed), blade mixing (slow-setting liquids, watch for 'additive balls')
Aeration: emulsions compact when they 'break' (brown-to-black); cutback asphalt aerates until volatile content ~50% of original and moisture <= 2%
Spreading/compacting: layers no thinner than ~1.5x max particle size, immediate pneumatic-tire rolling per layer, steel-wheel finish roll
sections.applicability: The complete field construction sequence for mixed-in-place bituminous/polymer stabilization, from windrow setup through finish rolling.

sections.title: Central Plant Mix Construction
sections.summary: Batch-type pugmills (>=2,000 lb capacity) or continuous-mixing plants (interlocked automatic feeders) proportion and mix asphalt/aggregate/water; windrow-deposited mixes are aerated by grader blading or rotary tiller; spread by paver (no aeration needed) or grader/spreader (deep lifts).
sections.body: PREPARATION OF MIXTURE: batch-type plants typically use a twin-shafted pugmill (capacity >= 2,000 lb / 907 kg); correct asphalt/aggregate amounts (usually by weight) are fed in, mixed, and discharged to a haul truck before the next batch. Continuous-mixing plants interlock asphalt/aggregate/water feeders to automatically maintain correct proportions, with automatic aggregate feeders governed by the output of a positive-displacement asphalt-metering pump and a spray-nozzle arrangement distributing asphalt over the aggregate. AERATING PLANT MIX: mixtures requiring aeration are deposited on the roadbed in windrows, then spread with a motor grader and aerated by blading back and forth or by rotary tiller mixing equipment. SPREADING AND COMPACTING PLANT MIX: if aeration is not required (typical for plant-mixed emulsified asphalt), the mixture is most effectively spread with automatic-control asphalt pavers; for deep lifts, Jersey Spreaders, towed spreaders, cutter-trimmer-spreaders, or motor graders may be used. As with mixed-in-place, cold mixes gain stability as diluents evaporate, so lift thickness is limited by the rate of diluent loss (governed by asphalt type, diluent content, gradation, aggregate temperature, wind, ambient temperature, and humidity) -- local experience is the best guide. Spread uniformly starting farthest from the mixing plant; hauling over freshly placed material is not permitted except when required to complete the work.
key_points: Batch-type pugmill: minimum 2,000 lb (907 kg) capacity, twin-shafted, weight-proportioned batches
Continuous-mixing plant: interlocked automatic feeders maintain correct asphalt/aggregate/water proportions
Aerating: windrow-deposited mix spread by grader, aerated by blading back-and-forth or rotary tiller
Spreading: automatic-control pavers when no aeration is needed; Jersey Spreaders/towed spreaders/graders for deep lifts
Lift thickness is governed by diluent-loss rate (asphalt type, diluent content, gradation, temperature, wind, humidity) -- local experience is the best guide
sections.applicability: Applies to bituminous/polymer stabilized-soil construction using a central mixing plant rather than mixed-in-place equipment.

sections.title: Construction with Fibers
sections.summary: Fiber-placement equipment has not reached a commercial stage; fibers are typically placed manually (bagged, in a grid or lanes, like cement/lime) and spread uniformly, avoiding windy days. Mix with a rotary mixer (multiple passes); avoid post-mixing grading/moving where possible.
sections.body: Equipment for placing fibers has not reached a commercial stage. Generally, fibers are placed manually by spacing bags of discrete fibers in a grid pattern or by lanes, similar to the way bagged cement and lime are placed. Like cement, spread the fibers uniformly within the area; the backside of a rake helps, as the rake tines drag the fibers. Placing fibers on days with winds above 15 mph (24 km/h) is not recommended. Wetting the fibers after spreading helps hold them in place if necessary. Fibers are difficult to efficiently mix and may require multiple passes of a rotary mixer to achieve even dispersal (fibrillated fibers may need multiple passes to 'open' the fibrils). If using cement or lime, spread the dry material first, then follow with the fibers. It is very important to start with the soil well-prepared and properly graded to minimize or eliminate any post-mixing soil work, since working the fibrous soil after mixing can be very difficult; it is not recommended to grade or move the material unless absolutely necessary. Before compaction it can be moved with graders/rakes and mildly graded, but once compacted, grading the surface causes tears/rips that are hard to repair. After compaction, the material is best handled by remixing with a rotary mixer to loosen it before working the soil.
key_points: No commercial fiber-placement equipment exists; fibers are placed manually (bagged, grid or lane pattern)
Avoid placing fibers on windy days (> 15 mph / 24 km/h)
Mixing requires multiple rotary-mixer passes for even dispersal (fibrillated fibers need extra passes to 'open')
If combining with cement/lime, spread the dry additive first, then the fibers
Minimize post-mixing/post-compaction grading: once compacted, grading tears the fibrous surface and is hard to repair
sections.applicability: Applies to construction of fiber-reinforced (alone or combined) stabilized soil layers.
